answers.reasoning: Block 1 says the authors point out batching helps less as sentences get longer because memory limits how many long examples fit in a batch.

Block 6 says that without scaling, large d_k makes dot products large and pushes the softmax into regions with tiny gradients (stated as the authors' hunch). Block 8 shows the weights collapsing onto one key and Σp(1−p) falling towards zero.
answers.answer: When d_k is large, raw query-key dot products grow large and spread widely, so softmax saturates: nearly all weight lands on one key and gradients become tiny. Dividing by √d_k keeps scores on a similar scale regardless of dimension, so the softmax stays responsive and learning continues.

Block 15 settles it: self-attention costs O(n²·d) against O(n·d²) for recurrence, so it is cheaper only when n<d. For very long inputs the authors suggest restricting attention to a neighbourhood of size r.
answers.answer: Here n = 20,000 is far larger than d = 512, so full self-attention's n²·d cost (about 2×10¹¹) exceeds the recurrent layer's n·d² (about 5×10⁹) by roughly n/d, about forty times. The authors' remedy is restricted self-attention: each position attends only to a neighbourhood of size r, costing O(r·n·d), though the maximum path length grows to O(n/r).

Block 15's Table 1 discussion says self-attention needs O(1) sequential operations versus O(n) for recurrence, and that it is cheaper per layer only when n<d, so the colleague's 'whatever the input' claim is wrong; block 1 frames the bottleneck as sequential processing within a sentence.
Block 2 names reduced effective resolution from averaging. Block 10 describes heads attending in different subspaces. Block 22/23 (rows A) shows a single head scoring 0.9 BLEU below the best setting.
answers.answer: Each self-attention output is a weighted average over positions, and averaging blurs detail, which the authors call reduced effective resolution: a word needing both its subject and object gets them mixed together. Multi-head attention runs several smaller attentions in parallel, each with its own projections, so each head can track a different relation in its own subspace at about the same total cost. Evidence: in Table 3 row (A), a single head scores 24.9 BLEU on the development set versus 25.8 with 8 heads.
